title: Isaiah 47:1–15
context: After 46:1–13—Bel bows down and Nebo stoops, idols borne as burdens on weary beasts; Listen, O house of Jacob, borne from before birth; even to old age I will carry you; declaring the end from the beginning, my counsel shall stand; calling a bird of prey from the east; I will put salvation in Zion for Israel my glory—the word turns: Come down and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground without a throne, O daughter of the Chaldeans.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Historic words on Come down, O virgin daughter of Babylon, millstones and grinding, nakedness uncovered, Our Redeemer the Holy One of Israel, mistress of kingdoms no more, no mercy on the aged, I am and there is no one besides me, loss of children and widowhood, sorceries that cannot charm away disaster, stargazers wearied, stubble in the flame, and none to save—so each camp speaks in its own voice beside Isaiah 47:1–15.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Down—From thy throne. Virgin—So called, because she was tender and delicate. No throne—For thee. The empire is taken from thee, and translated to the Persians. Called—Be so. Millstones—Thou shalt be brought to the basest slavery, which grinding at the mill was esteemed. For this work was not performed by horses, as now it is, but by the labour of slaves and captives. Grind—Grind bread-corn into meal for thy master’s use. Uncover—Take off the ornaments wherewith such women as were of good quality used to cover and dress their heads. These are predictions of what they should be forced to do or suffer. Thigh—Gird up thy garments close and short about thee, that thou mayest be fit for travelling on foot, and for passing over those rivers, through which thou wilt be constrained to wade, in the way to the land of thy captivity. Uncovered—Either for want of raiment to cover it; or rather, by thine enemies in way of scorn and contumely. As a man—With moderation and gentleness, as those men who have not quite put off humanity use to do. Silent—Thro’ grief and shame, as mourners use to do. The lady—The chief and glory of all kingdoms. Polluted—I cast them away as an unclean thing. Into thine hand—To punish them. No mercy—Thou hast exceeded the bounds of thy commission. The ancient—Who besides their common calamity were afflicted with the miseries of old age, and therefore did require both pity and reverence. These things—Thy cruel usages of my people, and the heavy judgments which thou hadst reason to expect for them. Nor remember—Thou didst not consider what might and was likely to befal thee afterward. I am—Independent, and self-sufficient. None—Which is not either subject to me, or far inferior to me in power and glory. Shall not sit—I shall never want either a king or people to defend me. Perfection—In the highest degree. Trusted—Confidently expecting to preserve thyself by these and other wicked arts. None seeth—My counsels are so deeply laid. Perverted—Hath misled thee into the way of perdition. None seeth—Which is repeated, to denote their intolerable self-confidence. Therefore—This agrees with the history. Babylon being surprized by Cyrus, when they were in deep security. Stand—Persist in these practices. Laboured—From the beginning of thy kingdom. For the Chaldeans in all ages were famous for the practice of these arts. Wearied—Thou hast spent thy time and strength in going from one to another, and all to no purpose. Thus—Such comfortless and helpless creatures. They—Merchants who came from several countries to trade with Babylon. And the verse may be thus rendered; Thus (vain and unprofitable) shall they (thy sorcerers) with whom thou hast laboured be unto thee: also thy merchants shall wander every one to his own quarter.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Isa 47:1–15)

reformed.quote: Explains the counsel of God: overthrow of Babylon and deliverance of the people connected; Babylon’s rank was a grave for the Jews. Imperative Come down more forceful—as from the judgment-seat (Jer 1:10). Virgin daughter: not modest or chaste, but brought up softly, never forced by enemies (as formerly of Sidon). Venice is illustration only; historic Babylon, not a newspaper. Great change: highest honor to lowest disgrace. Millstones: marks of degrading slavery; meanest slaves shut up in a mill. Unbind curled locks; uncover limbs to cross rivers. Baseness discovered when wealth’s veils are removed (Demosthenes on cities—illustration). I will take vengeance and will not meet a man: some supply “as a man”—you do not deal with man whose attack you can resist; others “I will not allow a man to meet me” as intercessor. Calvin prefers the former as smoother; either way the Lord will destroy the Babylonians and there will be no room for mercy. Our Redeemer: punishment of Babylon is for the salvation of his people (Isa 45:4). Holy One of Israel: not in vain he chose this people. Jehovah of Hosts. Sit silent: shame; contrast with her former loud commands over the East. Lady of kingdoms no more; Babylonian monarchy very widely extended. I was angry with my people: captivity is God’s scourge; he who struck will heal. Babylonians seized the occasion for cruelty, as if one became the executioner of a child a father had put into his hands to be chastised. I profaned my heritage: not a change of purpose so as to cast away the covenant; still his people; elect do not perish. Not in their power actually to go beyond the limit God assigned, but he looked at their cruelty (Zech 1:15). They did not spare even the aged. Thou saidst I shall for ever be a mistress: haughtiness of perpetual dominion; children of this world intoxicated by prosperity. Didst not remember her end: the end of Jerusalem. Delicate woman. I am, and there is none besides me: only God can truly say I AM (Ex 3:14); Babylon by this made war with God. Two things suddenly: widowhood and childlessness in perfection. For or in the multitude of divinations: either cause or notwithstanding; they trusted such delusions and dreaded nothing. Trustedst in thy malice: fraud and oppression by which they enlarged the kingdom; great kingdoms are great robberies. Blasphemies repeated. Sudden destruction when they say Peace (1 Thess 5:3); Daniel 5:30—Babylon taken in a night. Stand now amidst thy divinations: do as thou art wont; in the end the event will instruct. Alludes to augurs remaining unmoved till a sign is seen. Wearied in the multitude of counsels. Binders of the heavens, astrologers, monthly prognosticators. Judicial astrology versus prophets; fatal necessity of stars would extinguish divine predictions. Historic Chaldean arts. They shall be as stubble; fire consumes; not wood for heat but useless stubble. Traffickers and dealers, chiefly the diviners, from thy youth. Every one to his quarter: flight, with allusion to quarters of the heavens they divide. None shall save thee.

verses.text: Come down and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground without a throne, O daughter of the Chaldeans! For you shall no more be called tender and delicate.
verses.arminianNotes:
Come down and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground without a throne, O daughter of the Chaldeans! For you shall no more be called tender and delicate. Wesley: Down—From thy throne. Virgin—So called, because she was tender and delicate. No throne—For thee. The empire is taken from thee, and translated to the Persians. Called—Be so.

Arminian hearing: she comes down from the throne; virgin names her tender and delicate, not chaste; the empire is taken and translated to the Persians; she shall no more be called tender and delicate. Shared: Come down, O virgin daughter of Babylon; sit without a throne, O daughter of the Chaldeans; throne gone to the Persians. Historic Babylon, not a newspaper, not a living city or state, not a millennial camp fight. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “Down—From thy throne” and “Called—Be so” are his lemmas for “Come down” and “you shall no more be called.” Prefer no keyContrast on 1: both camps take historic Babylon coming down; skip Calvin’s Venice illustration rather than invent a newspaper fight. Match 46:1: Bel and Nebo already bowing. Match v. 5: mistress of kingdoms no more.
verses.reformedNotes:
Come down and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon. Calvin: explains the counsel of God—overthrow of Babylon and deliverance of the people connected; Babylon’s rank was a grave for the Jews. Imperative Come down more forceful, as from the judgment-seat (Jer 1:10). Virgin daughter: not modest or chaste, but brought up softly, never forced by enemies (as formerly of Sidon). His Venice illustration is illustration only—historic Babylon, not a newspaper.

Reformed hearing: Come down is the judgment-seat’s sentence; virgin is soft upbringing, not chastity; overthrow of Babylon and Israel’s deliverance are one counsel. Shared with Wesley: historic Babylon; throne gone; tender and delicate no more. Historic Babylon, not a newspaper, not a living city or state. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “Come down” and “virgin daughter” name the ESV lemmas. Prefer no keyContrast on 1: both historic Babylon; Venice is illustration, not the verse’s referent. Match 46:1: Bel and Nebo stoop. Match v. 2: millstones after the throne is gone.

verses.text: Take the millstones and grind flour, put off your veil, strip off your robe, uncover your legs, pass through the rivers.
verses.arminianNotes:
Take the millstones and grind flour, put off your veil, strip off your robe, uncover your legs, pass through the rivers. Wesley: Millstones—Thou shalt be brought to the basest slavery, which grinding at the mill was esteemed. For this work was not performed by horses, as now it is, but by the labour of slaves and captives. Grind—Grind bread-corn into meal for thy master’s use. Uncover—Take off the ornaments wherewith such women as were of good quality used to cover and dress their heads. These are predictions of what they should be forced to do or suffer. Thigh—Gird up thy garments close and short about thee, that thou mayest be fit for travelling on foot, and for passing over those rivers, through which thou wilt be constrained to wade, in the way to the land of thy captivity.

Arminian hearing: mill-slavery, not horse-mills; grind meal for a master; ornaments off; garments girt short to wade rivers toward captivity. Shared: millstones; grind flour; veil and robe off; legs uncovered; pass through the rivers. Historic Babylon’s fall into slavery, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “Thigh” is his lemma for ESV “uncover your legs”; “Grind bread-corn” for “grind flour.” Prefer no keyContrast: both hear highest honor to mill-slavery. Match v. 1: throne gone, then the mill. Match v. 3: nakedness uncovered.
verses.reformedNotes:
Take the millstones and grind flour. Calvin: great change—highest honor to lowest disgrace. Millstones: marks of degrading slavery; meanest slaves shut up in a mill. Unbind curled locks; uncover limbs to cross rivers.

Reformed hearing: from throne to mill; curled locks unbound; limbs uncovered to wade. Shared with Wesley: mill-slavery; ornaments off; rivers crossed on the way down. Historic Babylon, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “unbind curled locks” and “uncover limbs to cross rivers” name ESV “put off your veil” and “uncover your legs, pass through the rivers.” Prefer no keyContrast. Match v. 1: Come down from the throne. Match v. 3: disgrace seen.

verses.text: Your nakedness shall be uncovered, and your disgrace shall be seen. I will take vengeance, and I will spare no one.
verses.arminianNotes:
Your nakedness shall be uncovered, and your disgrace shall be seen. I will take vengeance, and I will spare no one. Wesley: Uncovered—Either for want of raiment to cover it; or rather, by thine enemies in way of scorn and contumely. As a man—With moderation and gentleness, as those men who have not quite put off humanity use to do.

Arminian hearing: nakedness uncovered by enemies in scorn; he will not meet her as a man—with moderation and gentleness; no humanity left in the stroke. Shared: nakedness uncovered; disgrace seen; I will take vengeance; no mercy. Historic Babylon, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: ESV “I will spare no one” is KJV “I will not meet thee as a man”; Wesley comments the KJV lemma “As a man,” not a different verse. Prefer no keyContrast on 3: lexical as-a-man versus spare-no-one is one no-mercy; do not fork. No open theism: he will take vengeance; he will spare no one. Match v. 2: legs uncovered, then nakedness. Match v. 4: Our Redeemer is the one who takes vengeance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Your nakedness shall be uncovered, and your disgrace shall be seen. I will take vengeance, and I will spare no one. Calvin: baseness discovered when wealth’s veils are removed (Demosthenes on cities—illustration, not a newspaper). I will take vengeance and will not meet a man: some supply “as a man”—you do not deal with man whose attack you can resist; others “I will not allow a man to meet me” as intercessor. Calvin prefers the former as smoother; either way the Lord will destroy the Babylonians and there will be no room for mercy.

Reformed hearing: veils of wealth fall; vengeance meets no man; no room for mercy. Shared with Wesley: nakedness uncovered; vengeance; no mercy. Historic Babylon, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: ESV “I will spare no one” is KJV “I will not meet thee as a man”; Calvin comments that KJV lemma, not a different English Bible. Prefer no keyContrast on 3: both no mercy; as-a-man versus spare-no-one is lexical, not a camp fork. No open theism: I will take vengeance; I will spare no one. Match v. 2: mill and uncovered legs. Match v. 4: the Redeemer who takes this vengeance.

verses.text: Our Redeemer—the LORD of hosts is his name—is the Holy One of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
Our Redeemer—the LORD of hosts is his name—is the Holy One of Israel. Wesley has no extra lemma. Paraphrase from v. 3 honestly: As a man—with moderation and gentleness he will not meet her; I will take vengeance, and I will spare no one. So here: Our Redeemer—the LORD of hosts is his name—is the Holy One of Israel, the same who takes that vengeance. Do not invent unique Wesley sentences.

Arminian hearing: the Redeemer named here is the Holy One who in v. 3 takes vengeance and will not meet as a man. Shared: Our Redeemer; the LORD of hosts is his name; the Holy One of Israel. Historic Redeemer of Israel, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: ESV’s em-dash names him in one breath—Our Redeemer—the LORD of hosts is his name—is the Holy One of Israel. Prefer no keyContrast: Wesley has no extra lemma; skip rather than invent. Match v. 3: I will take vengeance. Match v. 5: he silences the lady of kingdoms. Match 45:4: for Jacob my servant’s sake.
verses.reformedNotes:
Our Redeemer—the LORD of hosts is his name—is the Holy One of Israel. Calvin: Our Redeemer—punishment of Babylon is for the salvation of his people (Isa 45:4). Holy One of Israel: not in vain he chose this people. Jehovah of Hosts.

Reformed hearing: Babylon’s fall is Israel’s redemption; he chose this people not in vain; Jehovah of Hosts is his name. Shared with Wesley: Our Redeemer; the LORD of hosts; the Holy One of Israel. Historic Redeemer of Israel, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “Jehovah of Hosts” is his lemma for ESV “the LORD of hosts.” Prefer no keyContrast: Wesley has no extra lemma; skip rather than invent. Match 45:4: for Jacob my servant and Israel my chosen. Match v. 3: vengeance. Match v. 6: I was angry with my people, yet they remain his.

verses.text: Sit in silence, and go into darkness, O daughter of the Chaldeans; for you shall no more be called the mistress of kingdoms.
verses.arminianNotes:
Sit in silence, and go into darkness, O daughter of the Chaldeans; for you shall no more be called the mistress of kingdoms. Wesley: Silent—Thro’ grief and shame, as mourners use to do. The lady—The chief and glory of all kingdoms.

Arminian hearing: silence is grief and shame of mourners; she is no more the lady, the chief and glory of all kingdoms. Shared: Sit in silence; go into darkness; daughter of the Chaldeans; mistress of kingdoms no more. Historic Babylon, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: ESV “mistress of kingdoms” is Wesley’s “lady of kingdoms,” not a different verse; “Silent—Thro’ grief and shame” is his lemma for “Sit in silence”; “Thro’” is his spelling. Prefer no keyContrast: both hear the lady silenced. Match v. 1: no more called tender and delicate. Match v. 7: I shall be mistress forever—the boast this verse strips.
verses.reformedNotes:
Sit in silence, and go into darkness, O daughter of the Chaldeans. Calvin: Sit silent—shame; contrast with her former loud commands over the East. Lady of kingdoms no more; Babylonian monarchy very widely extended.

Reformed hearing: silence after loud command; the widely extended monarchy is lady no more. Shared with Wesley: Sit in silence; darkness; mistress/lady of kingdoms no more. Historic Babylon, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “Lady of kingdoms” is his lemma for ESV “mistress of kingdoms.” Prefer no keyContrast. Match v. 1: Come down, no throne. Match v. 7: the forever-mistress boast.

verses.text: I was angry with my people; I profaned my heritage; I gave them into your hand; you showed them no mercy; on the aged you made your yoke exceedingly heavy.
verses.arminianNotes:
I was angry with my people; I profaned my heritage; I gave them into your hand; you showed them no mercy; on the aged you made your yoke exceedingly heavy. Wesley: Polluted—I cast them away as an unclean thing. Into thine hand—To punish them. No mercy—Thou hast exceeded the bounds of thy commission. The ancient—Who besides their common calamity were afflicted with the miseries of old age, and therefore did require both pity and reverence.

Arminian hearing: he gave them into Babylon’s hand to punish them; she exceeded the bounds of that commission; the aged required pity and reverence and got a heavy yoke. Shared: I was angry with my people; I gave them into your hand; you showed them no mercy; heavy yoke on the aged. Historic Babylon and historic Israel, not a millennial camp fight. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “Polluted” is his lemma for ESV “I profaned my heritage”; “The ancient” for “the aged.” No open theism: I was angry; I gave them into your hand. Match v. 3: I will take vengeance. Match v. 7: these things—the cruel usages—not laid to heart.
verses.reformedNotes:
I was angry with my people; I profaned my heritage; I gave them into your hand; you showed them no mercy; on the aged you made your yoke exceedingly heavy. Calvin: I was angry with my people—anticipation; captivity is God’s scourge; he who struck will heal. Babylonians seized the occasion for cruelty, as if one became the executioner of a child a father had put into his hands to be chastised. Hence they have no right to be proud. I profaned my heritage: not a change of purpose so as to cast away the covenant; still his people; anger in Scripture refers to us who provoke, not to an emotion that stops his love; elect do not perish. How could they go beyond the limit God assigned? Not in their power actually to go beyond the limit, but he looked at their cruelty—they endeavored utterly to ruin those who had surrendered (Zech 1:15; James 2:13). On the old man: they did not spare even the aged.

Reformed hearing: scourge then heal; executioner of a child; not actually beyond the assigned limit, but cruelty of intent counted; covenant not cast away; elect do not perish. Shared with Wesley: I was angry with my people; I gave them into your hand; you showed them no mercy; heavy yoke on the aged. Historic Babylon and historic Israel, not a millennial camp fight. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “I profaned my heritage” names the ESV; “the old man” is his lemma for “the aged.” No open theism: he who struck will heal; anger is not a change of purpose. Match v. 4: still the Holy One of Israel. Match v. 7: she did not remember their end.
verses.keyContrast: Arminian readings, with Wesley, take “No mercy” as Thou hast exceeded the bounds of thy commission; Into thine hand—To punish them; the ancient required pity and reverence. Reformed readings, with Calvin, take the Babylonians as seizing the occasion for cruelty like an executioner of a child a father had put into their hands; not in their power actually to go beyond the limit God assigned, but he looked at their cruelty of intent (Zech 1:15); he who struck will heal; elect do not perish; anger is not a change of purpose so as to cast away the covenant. Shared: I was angry with my people; I gave them into your hand; you showed them no mercy; heavy yoke on the aged. Historic Babylon and historic Israel, not a millennial camp fight.

verses.text: You said, “I shall be mistress forever,” so that you did not lay these things to heart or remember their end.
verses.arminianNotes:
You said, “I shall be mistress forever,” so that you did not lay these things to heart or remember their end. Wesley: These things—Thy cruel usages of my people, and the heavy judgments which thou hadst reason to expect for them. Nor remember—Thou didst not consider what might and was likely to befal thee afterward.

Arminian hearing: the forever-mistress boast refused to lay the cruel usages and coming judgments to heart; she did not consider what might befal her afterward. Shared: I shall be mistress forever; these things not laid to heart; their end not remembered. Historic Babylon, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “These things—cruel usages” and “Nor remember—befal thee afterward” are his lemmas for “you did not lay these things to heart or remember their end”; “befal” is his spelling. Prefer no keyContrast: both hear the haughty forever-mistress; do not millennial-fight Calvin’s Church. Match v. 5: mistress of kingdoms no more. Match v. 6: the cruel usages of no mercy.
verses.reformedNotes:
You said, “I shall be mistress forever.” Calvin: Thou saidst I shall for ever be a mistress—haughtiness of perpetual dominion; children of this world intoxicated by prosperity. Say = conclude in one’s own mind. Didst not remember her end: the end of Jerusalem, the Church; they mock calamities of good men. Do not millennial-fight Church—historic Jerusalem under the yoke of v. 6.

Reformed hearing: perpetual-dominion boast; end of Jerusalem not remembered; prosperity intoxicated them. Shared with Wesley: I shall be mistress forever; these things not laid to heart; their end forgotten. Historic Babylon over historic Jerusalem, not a newspaper, not a millennial camp fight. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “I shall for ever be a mistress” is his lemma for ESV “I shall be mistress forever.” Prefer no keyContrast on 7: skip Church-as-Jerusalem rather than invent a millennial fork. Match v. 5: lady of kingdoms no more. Match v. 8: I am, and there is no one besides me.

verses.text: Now therefore hear this, you lover of pleasures, who sit securely, who say in your heart, “I am, and there is no one besides me; I shall not sit as a widow or know the loss of children”:
verses.arminianNotes:
Now therefore hear this, you lover of pleasures, who sit securely, who say in your heart, “I am, and there is no one besides me; I shall not sit as a widow or know the loss of children.” Wesley: I am—Independent, and self-sufficient. None—Which is not either subject to me, or far inferior to me in power and glory. Shall not sit—I shall never want either a king or people to defend me.

Arminian hearing: I am is independent self-sufficiency; none besides is none subject or none equal in power and glory; she will never want king or people. Shared: lover of pleasures; sit securely; I am, and there is no one besides me; not a widow, no loss of children. Historic Babylon, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “I am—Independent, and self-sufficient” is his lemma for “I am, and there is no one besides me.” Prefer no keyContrast on 8: both hear the pride of I am; Calvin’s Ex 3:14 is thicker, not a different verse. Match 46:9: I am God, and there is no other—the name she steals. Match v. 9: widowhood and loss of children in one day. Match v. 10: the I am repeated.
verses.reformedNotes:
Now therefore hear this, you lover of pleasures, who sit securely. Calvin: delicate woman. I am, and there is none besides me: only God can truly say I AM (Ex 3:14); Babylon by this made war with God. I shall not sit as a widow.

Reformed hearing: the delicate secure woman claims I AM, the name that is God’s alone; the boast is war with God. Shared with Wesley: I am, and there is no one besides me; not a widow; lover of pleasures sitting securely. Historic Babylon, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “I am, and there is none besides me” names the ESV; Ex 3:14 thickens the same pride, not a different verse. Prefer no keyContrast on 8: both camps hear the pride of I am; do not fork on Calvin’s thicker I AM. Match 45:5: I am the LORD, and there is no other. Match 46:9: none like me. Match v. 10: blasphemies repeated.

verses.text: These two things shall come to you in a moment, in one day; the loss of children and widowhood shall come upon you in full measure, in spite of your many sorceries and the great power of your enchantments.
verses.arminianNotes:
These two things shall come to you in a moment, in one day; the loss of children and widowhood shall come upon you in full measure, in spite of your many sorceries and the great power of your enchantments. Wesley: Perfection—In the highest degree.

Arminian hearing: the two things come in a moment, in one day, in the highest degree—loss of children and widowhood—despite the sorceries. Shared: two things in a moment, in one day; loss of children and widowhood; many sorceries and enchantments. Historic Babylon, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “Perfection—In the highest degree” is his lemma for ESV “in full measure.” Prefer no keyContrast: both hear sudden widowhood and childlessness in full. Match v. 8: I shall not sit as a widow. Match v. 11: ruin suddenly.
verses.reformedNotes:
These two things shall come to you in a moment, in one day. Calvin: two things suddenly—widowhood and childlessness in perfection. For/in the multitude of divinations: either cause or notwithstanding; Calvin: they trusted such delusions and dreaded nothing.

Reformed hearing: widowhood and childlessness in perfection, suddenly; they trusted the delusions and dreaded nothing. Shared with Wesley: two things in a moment; loss of children and widowhood in full/perfection; sorceries. Historic Babylon, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: ESV “in spite of” is Calvin’s “notwithstanding” option on the particle; “in full measure” is his “in perfection,” not a different verse. Prefer no keyContrast: cause-versus-notwithstanding is Calvin’s particle option, not a fight with Wesley’s thin Perfection. Match v. 8: the widow-boast. Match v. 12: stand fast in those enchantments.

verses.text: You felt secure in your wickedness; you said, “No one sees me”; your wisdom and your knowledge led you astray, and you said in your heart, “I am, and there is no one besides me.”
verses.arminianNotes:
You felt secure in your wickedness; you said, “No one sees me”; your wisdom and your knowledge led you astray, and you said in your heart, “I am, and there is no one besides me.” Wesley: Trusted—Confidently expecting to preserve thyself by these and other wicked arts. None seeth—My counsels are so deeply laid. Perverted—Hath misled thee into the way of perdition. None seeth—Which is repeated, to denote their intolerable self-confidence.

Arminian hearing: trusted wicked arts to preserve herself; no one sees—counsels deeply laid; wisdom perverted her into perdition; the none-seeth and I-am repeated for intolerable self-confidence. Shared: felt secure in wickedness; No one sees me; wisdom led astray; I am, and there is no one besides me. Historic Babylon, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “Trusted” is his lemma for ESV “You felt secure”; “Perverted” for “led you astray”; “None seeth” for “No one sees me.” Prefer no keyContrast: both hear the repeated I am and the unseen-counsel boast. Match v. 8: the same I am. Match v. 11: evil they cannot charm away.
verses.reformedNotes:
You felt secure in your wickedness; you said, “No one sees me.” Calvin: Trustedst in thy malice—fraud and oppression by which they enlarged the kingdom; great kingdoms are great robberies. Thou saidst, No one seeth me. I, and there is none beside me: blasphemies repeated.

Reformed hearing: security in malice; empire as robbery; no one sees; the I-am blasphemy said again. Shared with Wesley: felt secure in wickedness; No one sees me; I am, and there is no one besides me. Historic Babylon, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “Trustedst in thy malice” is his lemma for ESV “You felt secure in your wickedness”; “No one seeth me” for “No one sees me.” Prefer no keyContrast. Match v. 8: I am repeated. Match 46:9: the name that is God’s alone.

verses.text: But evil shall come upon you, which you will not know how to charm away; disaster shall fall upon you, for which you will not be able to atone; and ruin shall come upon you suddenly, of which you know nothing.
verses.arminianNotes:
But evil shall come upon you, which you will not know how to charm away; disaster shall fall upon you, for which you will not be able to atone; and ruin shall come upon you suddenly, of which you know nothing. Wesley: Therefore—This agrees with the history. Babylon being surprized by Cyrus, when they were in deep security.

Arminian hearing: the evil, disaster, and ruin match the history—Babylon surprized by Cyrus in deep security; they cannot charm it away or atone. Shared loudly with Calvin: historic Cyrus surprise in deep security; ruin suddenly. Historic Babylon taken by Cyrus, not a newspaper, not a living city. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “Therefore—This agrees with the history” and “surprized” are his lemma and spelling for the sudden ruin of the ESV. Prefer no keyContrast on 11: both historic Cyrus surprise; do not fork. No open theism: ruin shall come suddenly as he said; they know nothing of it because he said they would not. Match 46:11: bird of prey from the east. Match v. 9: in a moment, in one day. Match v. 8: who sit securely.
verses.reformedNotes:
But evil shall come upon you, which you will not know how to charm away; disaster shall fall upon you, for which you will not be able to atone; and ruin shall come upon you suddenly, of which you know nothing. Calvin: sudden destruction when they say Peace (1 Thess 5:3); Daniel 5:30—Babylon taken in a night. Shared with Wesley’s Cyrus surprise in deep security. Historic, not a newspaper.

Reformed hearing: Peace, then a night; Daniel 5:30; they cannot charm or atone. Shared loudly with Wesley: historic Cyrus surprise in deep security; ruin suddenly. Historic Babylon, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “ruin—suddenly” names the ESV; 1 Thess 5:3 and Dan 5:30 illustrate the same night, not a different verse. Prefer no keyContrast on 11: both historic Cyrus surprise; skip rather than invent. No open theism: ruin comes suddenly as he said. Match 46:11: Cyrus the bird from the east. Match v. 9: two things in a moment. Match v. 12: charm and sorcery cannot stand.

verses.text: Stand fast in your enchantments and your many sorceries, with which you have labored from your youth; perhaps you may be able to succeed; perhaps you may inspire terror.
verses.arminianNotes:
Stand fast in your enchantments and your many sorceries, with which you have labored from your youth; perhaps you may be able to succeed; perhaps you may inspire terror. Wesley: Stand—Persist in these practices. Laboured—From the beginning of thy kingdom. For the Chaldeans in all ages were famous for the practice of these arts.

Arminian hearing: persist in the arts; laboured from the beginning of the kingdom; Chaldeans famous in all ages for them; the perhaps is taunt. Shared: Stand fast in enchantments and many sorceries; labored from youth; perhaps succeed, perhaps inspire terror. Historic Chaldean arts, not a newspaper horoscope. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “Stand—Persist” and “Laboured—From the beginning of thy kingdom” are his lemmas for “Stand fast” and “labored from your youth.” Prefer no keyContrast. Match v. 9: many sorceries. Match v. 13: wearied with many counsels.
verses.reformedNotes:
Stand fast in your enchantments and your many sorceries. Calvin: Stand now amidst thy divinations—do as thou art wont; in the end the event will instruct. Alludes to augurs remaining unmoved till a sign is seen.

Reformed hearing: keep standing as the augurs stand; the event will instruct; perhaps is taunt. Shared with Wesley: Stand fast in the old Chaldean arts; labored from youth. Historic Chaldean divinations, not a newspaper horoscope. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “Stand now amidst thy divinations” is his lemma for ESV “Stand fast in your enchantments.” Prefer no keyContrast. Match v. 11: they cannot charm evil away. Match v. 13: let the star-gazers stand forth and save.

verses.text: You are wearied with your many counsels; let them stand forth and save you, those who divide the heavens, who gaze at the stars, who at the new moons make known what shall come upon you.
verses.arminianNotes:
You are wearied with your many counsels; let them stand forth and save you, those who divide the heavens, who gaze at the stars, who at the new moons make known what shall come upon you. Wesley: Wearied—Thou hast spent thy time and strength in going from one to another, and all to no purpose.

Arminian hearing: time and strength spent going from counselor to counselor, all to no purpose; let them stand forth and save—they cannot. Shared: wearied with many counsels; dividers of the heavens; star-gazers; new-moon prognosticators. Historic Chaldean arts, not a newspaper horoscope column. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “Wearied—going from one to another, all to no purpose” is his lemma for “You are wearied with your many counsels.” Prefer no keyContrast. Match v. 12: labored from youth in sorceries. Match v. 14: they are stubble.
verses.reformedNotes:
You are wearied with your many counsels; let them stand forth and save you, those who divide the heavens, who gaze at the stars, who at the new moons make known what shall come upon you. Calvin: Wearied in the multitude of counsels. Binders of the heavens / astrologers / monthly prognosticators. Judicial astrology versus prophets; fatal necessity of stars would extinguish divine predictions. Historic Chaldean arts, not a newspaper horoscope column.

Reformed hearing: binders of the heavens, astrologers, monthly prognosticators wearied and unable to save; the stars’ necessity would cancel prophecy, and it will not. Shared with Wesley: wearied with many counsels; they cannot save. Historic Chaldean arts, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “Binders of the heavens” and “monthly prognosticators” are his lemmas for “those who divide the heavens” and “who at the new moons make known.” Prefer no keyContrast. Match v. 12: stand in the enchantments. Match v. 14: stubble in the flame. Match 46:10: my counsel shall stand.

verses.text: Behold, they are like stubble; the fire consumes them; they cannot deliver themselves from the power of the flame. No coal for warming oneself is this, no fire to sit before!
verses.arminianNotes:
Behold, they are like stubble; the fire consumes them; they cannot deliver themselves from the power of the flame. No coal for warming oneself is this, no fire to sit before! Wesley has no extra lemma. Paraphrase from v. 13 honestly: Wearied—Thou hast spent thy time and strength in going from one to another, and all to no purpose. So here: Behold, they are like stubble; the fire consumes them—the same wearied counselors cannot deliver themselves from the flame. Paraphrase from v. 15: Thus—Such comfortless and helpless creatures. Do not invent unique Wesley sentences.

Arminian hearing: the wearied counselors of v. 13 are stubble, not a hearth; no coal to warm, no fire to sit before; they cannot deliver themselves. Shared: like stubble; the fire consumes them; they cannot deliver themselves; no coal, no fire to sit before. Historic Chaldean counselors, not a newspaper. Prefer no keyContrast: Wesley has no extra lemma; skip rather than invent. Match v. 13: wearied, cannot save. Match v. 15: none to save you.
verses.reformedNotes:
Behold, they are like stubble; the fire consumes them; they cannot deliver themselves from the power of the flame. No coal for warming oneself is this, no fire to sit before! Calvin: they shall be as stubble; fire consumes; not wood for heat but useless stubble.

Reformed hearing: not a hearth-fire but consuming flame; useless stubble, no coal to warm, no fire to sit before. Shared with Wesley: stubble; fire consumes; they cannot deliver themselves. Historic Chaldean arts burned, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “as stubble; fire consumes; not wood for heat but useless stubble” names ESV “like stubble” and “No coal for warming oneself is this, no fire to sit before.” Prefer no keyContrast: Wesley has no extra lemma. Match v. 13: the star-gazers. Match v. 15: none shall save thee.

verses.text: Such to you are those with whom you have labored, who have done business with you from your youth; they wander about, each in his own direction; there is no one to save you.
verses.arminianNotes:
Such to you are those with whom you have labored, who have done business with you from your youth; they wander about, each in his own direction; there is no one to save you. Wesley: Thus—Such comfortless and helpless creatures. They—Merchants who came from several countries to trade with Babylon. And the verse may be thus rendered; Thus (vain and unprofitable) shall they (thy sorcerers) with whom thou hast laboured be unto thee: also thy merchants shall wander every one to his own quarter.

Arminian hearing: comfortless, helpless; sorcerers vain and unprofitable; merchants from several countries wander each to his own quarter; no one to save. Shared: those with whom you labored from youth; they wander each his own way; there is no one to save you. Historic Babylon’s sorcerers and merchants, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “Thus—Such comfortless and helpless creatures” and “They—Merchants” are his lemmas for “Such to you are those with whom you have labored, who have done business with you”; he allows both sorcerers and merchants. Prefer no keyContrast: both hear none shall save. Match v. 12: labored from youth. Match v. 14: they cannot deliver themselves. Match v. 4: Our Redeemer is Israel’s, not Babylon’s.
verses.reformedNotes:
Such to you are those with whom you have labored, who have done business with you from your youth; they wander about, each in his own direction; there is no one to save you. Calvin: traffickers/dealers; chiefly the diviners; from thy youth. Every one to his quarter: flight, with allusion to quarters of the heavens they divide. None shall save thee.

Reformed hearing: the dealers are chiefly the diviners; flight to the quarters they used to divide; none shall save thee. Shared with Wesley: labored from youth; they wander each his own way; no one to save. Historic Babylon, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “traffickers/dealers; chiefly the diviners” and “every one to his quarter” are his lemmas for “who have done business with you” and “each in his own direction.” Prefer no keyContrast: Wesley’s sorcerers-and-merchants and Calvin’s diviners-chiefly overlap as none shall save. Match v. 13: divide the heavens. Match v. 14: stubble. Match 46:7: it does not answer or save.
